title: Ligand-dependent Wnt signaling promotes gastric cancer metastasis through hyaluronan expression in microenvironment

paper_content.abstract: The majority of gastric cancer cells proliferate in a Wnt ligand-dependent manner. To investigate this, we generated mice harboring Kras, Tgfbr2, and Trp53 (KTP) as well as with the same mutations plus Wnt1 expression (WKTP) in gastric mucosa. While KTP mice develop gastric metaplasia, WKTP mice develop dysplastic tumors, highlighting the role of ligand-dependent Wnt signaling in primary tumorigenesis. Organoids derived from WKTP mice form liver metastases following splenic transplantation, whereas KTP organoids do not. Notably, Apc disruption fails to induce metastasis of KTP cells, suggesting that stromal Wnt signaling promotes metastasis. Mechanistically, tumor-derived Wnt ligands cooperate with TGFβ signaling to induce Has2 expression in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), leading to hyaluronan accumulation in the metastatic microenvironment. Strikingly, hyaluronidase expression in WKTP cells significantly suppresses liver metastasis. Here we show the critical role of ligand-dependent Wnt signaling and Has2-mediated hyaluronan deposition in metastasis, offering potential therapeutic strategy against gastric cancer metastasis.
paper_content.introduction:
Gastric cancer is the fifth most common cancer worldwide and ranks third in cancer-related mortality1,2. The survival rate for patients with metastatic gastric cancer remains dismal, with a median survival of approximately three months, highlighting the urgent need for the development of preventive and therapeutic strategies against gastric cancer metastasis3,4. However, the mechanisms underlying gastric cancer metastasis are not fully understood.

Comprehensive genomic analyses have identified gene mutations involved in gastric cancer development, leading to its classification into four subtypes: Epstein-Barr virus-positive, microsatellite instability, genomically stable, and chromosomal instability (CIN) types5. Unlike colorectal cancer, where multi-step tumorigenesis is well-characterized, gastric cancer exhibits significant genetic heterogeneity6,7. While mutations in APC or CTNNB1, which activate canonical Wnt signaling, are present in 86% of non-hypermutated colorectal cancers, these mutations are less common in gastric cancer5,7. Nevertheless, Wnt signaling plays a critical role in maintaining normal tissue stem cells and is thought to be important for the development of various types of cancers, including gastric cancer8,9.

Recent analyses using gastric cancer-derived organoids have shown that Wnt signaling is activated in approximately 60% of gastric cancers through an exogenous ligand-dependent mechanism, despite the absence of APC or CTNNB1 mutation10. Elevated expression of Wnt ligand family genes, such as Wnt1, Wnt3a, and Wnt5a, as well as aberrant expression of Wnt receptors and co-receptors, has been identified in gastric cancer. These contribute to constitutive Wnt signaling activation9,11. The role of ligand-dependent Wnt signaling in gastric tumorigenesis has been previously reported. For instance, KLF3 is upregulated in gastric cancer, leading to increased Wnt1 expression, which promotes proliferation, migration, and metastasis of gastric cancer cells12. Gastric cancer cells disseminated in the peritoneal cavity express Wnt3a and Wnt5a in ascitic fluid, enhancing the colony-forming ability of dormant cancer cells13. Moreover, Wnt1 transgenic mice have been shown to develop glandular-type gastric tumors when inflammatory responses are present14,15. Despite these findings, the detailed role of ligand-dependent Wnt signaling in gastric cancer, particularly in metastasis, remains unclear.

Recently, a genetic mouse model for CIN-type gastric cancer was developed by introducing mutations in Kras, Tgfbr2, and Trp53 simultaneously in gastric epithelial cells using Anxa10 gene promoters16. This model develops invasive gastric adenocarcinomas with histological features similar to human CIN-type gastric cancers. However, the role of Wnt signaling was not examined in this model.

In this work, we analyze the role of ligand-dependent Wnt signaling in gastric cancer development and metastasis by generating novel mouse and organoid models. Using this system, we demonstrate that Wnt ligand expression in tumor cells is crucial for liver metastasis development. Tumor cell-secreting Wnt ligands activate stromal cells to express Has2, leading to the production and deposition of hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan) in the tumor microenvironment. This hyaluronan deposition is critical for the survival and colonization of disseminated cancer cells in the liver. These results suggest that targeting the ligand-dependent Wnt signaling or HAS2 expression in the stromal cells could serve as a potential preventive or therapeutic strategy against gastric cancer metastases.
paper_content.results:
Ligand-dependent Wnt signaling promotes gastric tumor formation
Kras activation, TGFβ suppression, and p53 mutation are major driver pathways in CIN-type or intestinal-type gastric cancer5,7. We generated compound mouse models, in which Kras+/G12D, Tgfbr2-/-, or Trp53+/R270H mutations were introduced in the gastric epithelial cells using Claudin18-CreERT2 mice17. In this study, we designated these model mice as K (Kras+/G12D), KT (Kras+/G12D, Tgfbr2-/-), KP (Kras+/G12D, Trp53+/R270H), and KTP (Kras+/G12D, Tgfbr2-/-, Trp53+/R270H) (Fig. 1a). It has been shown that Wnt signaling is activated in a ligand-dependent manner in more than half of gastric cancers9,10. We found upregulation of at least one of the Wnt ligand family member genes except Wnt8A in more than 80% of gastric cancers (Supplementary Fig. 1). In this study, we selected Wnt1 based on previous reports demonstrating a strong correlation between WNT1 expression and advanced grade of gastric cancer, and showing that WNT1-mediated signaling promotes the gastric tumor growth and metastasis12,18. We thus crossed the KT, KP, and KTP mice with K19-Wnt1 transgenic mice, which express Wnt1 in gastric epithelia, to generate WKT, WKP, and WKTP mice, respectively (Fig. 1a). K19-Wnt1 mice exhibit only limited dysplastic lesions in the gastric mucosa14,15.

All mutant mice except the simple Kras mutant group showed significantly increased gastric mucosal thickness compared with wild-type mice (Fig. 1b, c). In wild-type mice, Ki67-positive proliferating cells were confined to the gland neck, while in KT, KP, and KTP mice, they were significantly increased at the gland bottom of the glandular stomach (Fig. 1d). In WKT, WKP, and WKTP mice, Ki67-positive cells spanned entire glands, with a significantly increased Ki67 labeling index (Fig. 1d, e). These results indicate that the KrasG12D with Tgfbr2-/- or Trp53R270H mutations induce mucosal hyperplasia, with concurrent Wnt signaling activation further enhancing proliferation.

The KrasG12D mutation also impacted cell differentiation: H+/K+ ATPase-expressing parietal cells were lost in all mice carrying KrasG12D mutation, while Muc5AC-expressing mucous cells increased in the K, KT, KP, and KTP mouse glandular stomachs (Fig. 1f). Furthermore, dysplastic epithelial cells proliferated predominantly in the gastric mucosa of WKT, WKP, and WKTP mice, which was associated with decreased Muc5AC-expressing cells (Fig. 1b). Collectively, these results indicate that KrasG12D mutation induces hyperplasia and mucous cell metaplasia, whereas the combination of KrasG12D mutation and Wnt signaling activation leads to suppression of epithelial differentiation and the formation of dysplastic tumors (Supplementary Table 1).

KT, KTP, WKT, and WKTP mice that had KT mutations in their genotypes developed invasive tumors in the submucosa of the stomach, while such invasive tumors were not found in K, KP, WKP mice (Fig. 1b, g). Aggressive submucosal tumors with a collagen-rich fibrotic microenvironment formed in both KTP and WKTP mice (Fig. 1h). These results suggest that a combination of KrasG12D and Tgfbr2-/- (KT) mutations is sufficient for submucosal invasion, independent of Wnt ligand expression (Supplementary Table 1).

KTP mutations are sufficient for invasive tumor formation
We next established organoids from gastric epithelial cells of tamoxifen-untreated KTP and WKTP mice, and Kras, Tgfbr2, and Trp53 mutations were introduced in the organoids via tamoxifen treatment (Fig. 2a). As expected, KTP organoids could not survive or proliferate when Wnt ligands were removed from the culture medium, while WKTP organoids continued to proliferate, even without Wnt ligands in the medium (Fig. 2b, c). Notably, inhibition of Wnt ligand secretion using the PORCN inhibitor, C59, significantly suppressed proliferation of WKTP organoid cells. These results indicate that both KTP and WKTP cells require exogenous Wnt ligand stimulation for survival and proliferation, but WKTP cells utilize self-secreted Wnt ligands via autocrine or paracrine mechanisms (Fig. 2d).

We then injected KTP and WKTP organoid cells orthotopically into the submucosal area of the immunodeficient NSG mouse stomach (Fig. 2e). In vivo imaging analysis indicated that both KTP and WKTP cells developed tumors of similar sizes in the stomach (Fig. 2f, g). Histologically, dysplastic KTP and WKTP tumor cells proliferated in the submucosa of the stomach, and a fibrotic microenvironment was generated with αSMA-expressing fibroblasts (Fig. 2h). When KTP and WKTP organoid cells were transplanted subcutaneously, both organoids formed similar dysplastic tumors associated with a fibrotic microenvironment like orthotopic tumors (Supplementary Fig. 2). These results suggest that the combination of KTP driver mutations is sufficient to induce dysplastic tumor formation in both the submucosal and subcutaneous environments.

Wnt ligand expression is required for liver metastasis
We next evaluated the role of Wnt ligands in liver metastasis. In the orthotopic transplantation model of WKTP organoids, three of five mice exhibited signs of peritoneal dissemination by day 28, accompanied by clinical deterioration, which limited the observation window for assessing liver metastasis (Supplementary Fig. 3). We therefore performed spleen transplantation of KTP and WKTP organoids in NSG mice to examine the liver metastatic tumors (Fig. 3a).

Importantly, WKTP organoid cells formed large metastatic tumors in the liver, whereas KTP organoid cells did not develop detectable tumors in the liver (Fig. 3b, c). Histologically, metastatic tumors of the WKTP cells consisted of dysplastic and proliferating tumor cells, and a fibrotic microenvironment with αSMA-expressing cells was generated in the stroma (Fig. 3d, right). In contrast, KTP cells formed only small, scattered lesions, lacking a fibrotic microenvironment (Fig. 3d, left). No metastatic lesions were detected outside the liver in mice transplanted with either WKTP or KTP organoids.

Furthermore, treatment of mice with PORCN inhibitor ETC-159 significantly suppressed liver metastasis formation by WKTP cells (Fig. 3e, f). Another inhibitor, GNF-6231, also reduced tumor area, although the difference was not statistically significant. Histological analysis revealed that the remaining WKTP cells in the ETC-159-treated mouse livers were differentiated, forming enlarged cystic structures with decreased Ki67 labeling (Fig. 3g). These results, taken together, indicate that Wnt ligand expression is critical for the development of liver metastases in gastric cancer.

We next performed histological analysis to examine the early stages of liver metastasis development using GFP-labeled KTP and WKTP organoids. On day 3 after organoid transplantation to the spleen, both KTP and WKTP cells were detected in the liver sinusoids with similar efficiency (Fig. 3h). On day 7 after transplantation, numerous small metastatic lesions of WKTP cells were detected in the liver, accompanied by activated fibroblasts and infiltrating CD206+ M2-like macrophages (Fig. 3h, i, and Supplementary Fig. 4). In contrast, such metastatic lesions were rarely detected in livers transplanted with KTP cells. Therefore, it is possible that ligand-dependent Wnt signaling is critical for the colonization of the disseminated tumor cells during the early stage of liver metastasis.

Cell-intrinsic Wnt signaling is insufficient for metastasis
The Wnt ligands secreted by WKTP cells may activate Wnt signaling not only in tumor cells but also in stromal cells. To examine whether Wnt signaling activation in tumor cells alone is sufficient for metastasis, we disrupted the Apc gene in KTP cells using CRISPR/Cas9 to generate Apc-KTP cells (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 5). In Apc-KTP cells, Wnt signaling is expected to be constitutively activated in a ligand-independent manner due to homozygous Apc gene disruption, while Wnt signaling in surrounding stromal cells remains unaffected (Fig. 4b). As a control, we constructed Wnt1-expressing KTP cells, Wnt-KTP, by transfecting a Wnt1 expression vector into KTP cells.

Loss of APC suppresses phosphorylation-dependent β-catenin degradation, thereby increasing the unphosphorylated (active) form of β-catenin. The stabilized β-catenin translocates to the nucleus and functions with TCF/LEF to drive Wnt-target gene transcription. Consistent with this rationale, immunoblotting showed a significant increase in unphosphorylated β-catenin in Apc-KTP cells compared with KTP and WKTP cells (Fig. 4c), and the TOPFlash reporter assay demonstrated significantly higher β-catenin/TCF transcriptional activity in Apc-KTP cells, which is comparable to the Apc-disrupted intestinal tumor-derived organoids, AKTP19 (Fig. 4d). The Wnt activation level in Wnt-KTP cells was also increased, comparable to that in WKTP cells. However, proliferation rates and invasive capacities of Apc-KTP and Wnt-KTP cells were not changed from those of parental KTP cells (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b).

Subsequently, the Apc-KTP and Wnt-KTP cells were transplanted into the mouse spleen (Fig. 4e). We confirmed multiple metastatic tumors of WKTP cells in the livers, while no tumors were found in the KTP cell-transplanted mice (Fig. 4f, g). Among the three independently established Apc-KTP organoid lines, only line #2 developed limited, small macroscopic liver metastasis (Fig. 4f, arrowheads, Fig. 4g), whereas other lines showed no grossly detectable liver metastasis. Moreover, histological analysis revealed rare, small clusters of tumor cells in #2 and #8 Apc-KTP-transfected livers (Supplementary Fig. 6c), which were below the threshold of gross detection. In contrast, Wnt-KTP organoid cells formed visible liver tumors. These results indicate that cell-intrinsic Wnt signaling activation in tumor cells is insufficient for metastasis, suggesting that Wnt signaling activation in stromal cells is essential for liver metastasis.

Wnt signaling activation in CAFs of liver metastatic tumors
To investigate Wnt signaling activation in the tumor stroma, we performed spatial transcriptomic analysis (Visium) on histological sections of WKTP cell liver metastasis (Fig. 5a). RNA sequence data at 3,634 spots identified seven clusters, with cluster 7 excluded as it corresponded to necrotic areas (Fig. 5b). We next examined the expression of cell-type-specific marker genes. The hepatocyte marker Alb was significantly enriched in cluster 3 and 6, whereas Prom1 and Muc1, which are highly expressed in WKTP cells, were predominantly expressed in cluster 2 (Fig. 5c). On the other hand, myofibroblast markers, Acta2 and Tagln, were increased in cluster 4 and 5, and fibroblast markers, Pdgfrb and Col6a2 were increased in Cluster 5. H&E staining indicates that the major cell type in the cluster 5 area is fibroblastic cells of tumor stroma (Fig. 5d, enclosed with a white line in A), while both fibroblasts and tumor epithelial cells are mixed in the cluster 4 area (Fig. 5d, enclosed with a yellow line in B), indicating that CAFs are predominantly enriched in cluster 5. We confirmed αSMA expression in fibroblastic cells of cluster 5 area by immunohistochemistry (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Notably, cluster 5 was enriched with extracellular matrix (ECM) components, Eln, Dpt, Fbn1, Fbn2, Col1a2, Col3a1, Col6a2, Col8a1, and Col15a1, and ECM remodeling enzymes, Has2, Mmp2, Mmp23, and Adam19 (Supplementary Data 1). These results suggest dynamic remodeling of the fibrotic microenvironment in the liver metastatic tumors.

Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) using the cluster 5 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) revealed significant activation of Wnt signaling pathways including CTNNB1 and WNT3A, and TGFβ pathways, such as TGFB1, SMAD3, and SMAD4 (Fig. 5e). Consistently, we found nuclear accumulation of phosphorylated Smad2 in stromal cells of liver metastatic tumors (Supplementary Fig. 7b). We also confirmed both WKTP tumor cells and CAFs express TGFβ1 (Supplementary Fig. 7c). These findings suggest that WKTP cells serve as the primary source of TGFβ ligands, which in turn activate stromal cells to express TGFβ themselves, resulting in sustained activation of the TGFβ signaling pathway. Since TGFβ is crucial for generating a fibrotic microenvironment in the liver19,20, these findings suggest that tumor cell-secreting Wnt ligands activate Wnt signaling in CAFs, cooperating with TGFβ to promote metastatic microenvironment formation.

Wnt ligands activate stromal fibroblasts
It has been reported that CAFs in gastric cancer tissues can be classified into myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs) and inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs) based on distinct gene expression profiles21,22. Moreover, recent findings indicate that hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) have the potential to differentiate into both myCAFs and iCAFs23. However, it is also established that CAFs exhibit considerable heterogeneity in their cellular origins24. Therefore, to assess whether Wnt ligands activate stromal fibroblasts in the metastatic niche, we conducted experiments using both HSCs and CAFs, treating them with afamin-bound Wnt3a, which maintains stable canonical Wnt ligand activity25. (Fig. 6a). Afamin-Wnt3a treatment significantly increased Wnt signaling activation in both the HSCs and CAFs (Fig. 6b), and it also upregulated Wnt-target genes such as Axin2, Lef1, and Cd44 in HSCs (Fig. 6c). Additionally, expression of Acta2 encoding αSMA was also upregulated in HSCs by Afamin-Wnt3a, indicating that Wnt ligand-signaling activates stromal fibroblasts (Fig. 6d, e). Furthermore, combined treatment with afamin-Wnt3a and TGFβ synergistically enhanced HSC contraction in ECM gels (Fig. 6f), suggesting that Wnt and TGFβ signaling cooperatively activate HSCs, leading to activation of CAFs in the microenvironment.

Hyaluronan promotes metastatic tumor development
Among the genes upregulated in cluster 5, Has2, which encodes hyaluronan synthase, was identified (Supplementary Data 1). We confirmed that Has2 expression is specifically increased in cluster 5 of liver metastatic tumors of WKTP cells (Fig. 7a). A recent study indicates that hyaluronan plays an important role in the malignant progression of colon cancer26. Furthermore, Has2 expression in primary HSCs, imHSCs, and CAFs was significantly increased upon treatment with either afamin-Wnt3a or TGFβ. Notably, Has2 expression levels were dramatically elevated when HSCs and CAFs were simultaneously stimulated with both afamin-Wnt3a and TGFβ, indicating a synergistic effect of Wnt and TGFβ signaling in Has2 induction in stromal cells (Fig. 7b). We further examined HAS2 expression in human gastric cancer using the cBioPortal database (https://www.cbioportal.org/). As expected, there was a positive correlation between HAS2 and ECM component genes, including collagens (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Moreover, we observed a modest but positive correlation between HAS2 and canonical Wnt ligands such as WNT2, WNT2B, and WNT6 (the latter has been reported to act predominantly through the canonical Wnt signaling), suggesting a potential role for canonical Wnt signaling in the regulation of HAS2 expression in human gastric cancer (Supplementary Fig. 8b). Interestingly, there is also a positive correlation the non-canonical Wnt ligand WNT5A, suggesting a possible involvement of non-canonical Wnt signaling in HAS2 induction. We also detected significant hyaluronan deposition in the stroma of liver metastatic tumors of mouse and human gastric cancer (Fig. 7c, Supplementary Fig. 8c). It is of note that hyaluronan deposition was found from the early stage (day 7) of metastasis development.

We then examined the role of hyaluronan in liver metastasis development. To suppress hyaluronan deposition in the tumor stroma, we transfected expression vectors of hyaluronidases, Hyal1 and Hyal2, into WKTP cells to generate Hyal-WKTP cells (Fig. 7d). We anticipated that Hyal-WKTP cells, which co-express Hyal1 and Hyal2, would degrade both high molecular weight (HMW)- and low molecular weight (LMW)-hyaluronan within the tumor microenvironment27. Immunoblotting confirmed the expression of both Hyal1 and Hyal2 in Hyal-WKTP cells, and their expression did not affect the proliferation rate of WKTP cells (Supplementary Fig. 9a). Subsequently, Hyal-WKTP cells were transplanted into mouse spleens, and liver tissues were examined (Fig. 7e). Notably, metastatic tumor development was markedly suppressed in mice transplanted with Hyal-WKTP cells compared to those transplanted with parental WKTP cells (Fig. 7f, g). Interestingly, Hyal-WKTP cells formed tumors of a similar size at the spleen transplantation site as parental WKTP cells (Supplementary Fig. 9b). These results collectively indicate that hyaluronan deposition in the tumor stroma is crucial for the development of liver metastatic tumors in gastric cancer.
paper_content.methods:
Ethics statement
All experiments were conducted in compliance with all relevant ethical regulations. All animal experiments were performed with the protocol approved by the Committee on Animal Experimentation of Kanazawa University (approval no. AP-214223). The approved humane endpoints were based on clinical signs of deterioration or severe distress. Because tumor burden could not be measured in the orthotopic/splenic transplantation model, animals were euthanized if they exhibited ≥35% loss of body weight from baseline or inability to remain upright. For animals exhibiting 25–35% body weight loss, health checks were performed at least twice daily, and water-soaked food was provided on the cage floor to support hydration and nutrition. Animals meeting these criteria were euthanized immediately. All experiments using human samples were approved by the Human Genome/Gene Analysis Research Ethics Committee of Kanazawa University, and written informed consent was obtained from all patients.

Mouse strains
Tgfbr2flox/flox, Trp53+/LSL-R270H, and Kras+/LSL-G12D mice were obtained from the Mouse Repository (NCI-Frederick, Frederick, MD)42–44. K19-Wnt1 mice were previously constructed14,15. For induction of driver mutations in gastric epithelial cells, Claudin18-CreERT2 mice were used17. The genetic background of all mutant strains used in this study is C57BL/6. Mice were administered tamoxifen intraperitoneally (i.p.) at 4 mg/mouse at 6 weeks of age, and tumor phenotypes in the glandular stomach were evaluated 28 days after administration (n=3 mice for each genotype). Both male and female mice were used for examination. No significant sex-related differences were observed in tumor phenotypes.

Human samples
Three liver metastasis samples of gastric cancer were obtained from three male patients aged 45–78 years. No participant compensation was provided. These tissues were fixed in 10% buffered formalin, embedded in paraffin, and 4-μm sections were used for histological assessment and hyaluronan expression analysis. Human samples were limited to three male patients; therefore, sex-based analyses were not performed.

Histology and Immunohistochemistry
Tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 4-µm thickness. These sections were stained with H&E or processed for immunohistochemistry. Leica DM5000B (Leica) and BZ-9000 Biorevo (Keyence) were used to examine histology, immunohistochemistry (IHC), and fluorescence IHC.

The height of the gastric mucosa was measured on the H&E sections, and the relative mucosal thickness to the wild type was calculated. Tumor areas on the digital images of H&E sections were colored in yellow using an All-in-One microscope and BZ-II Analyzer (Keyence, Kanagawa, Japan), and the tumor areas were measured per field.

Primary antibodies used were anti-Ki67 (#ab16667, Abcam, Cambridge, UK; 1:1,000), anti-H+/K+-ATPase β subunit (#D032-3, MBL, Tokyo, Japan; 1:1000), anti-Muc5AC (#MS-145, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Grand Island, NY; 1:200), anti-αSMA (#A2547, SIGMA, St. Louis, MO; 1:800), anti-E-cadherin (#AF748, R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN; 1:100), anti-GFP (#2956, Cell Signaling, Danvers, MA; 1:500), anti-CD206 (#24595, Cell signaling, Danvers, MA; 1:200), anti-F4/80 (#MCA497, Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA; 1:500), and anti-phospho-Smad2 (#44-244G, Thermo Fisher Scientific; 1:400). The staining signals were visualized using an ImmPACT DAB Peroxidase Substrate Kit (#SK-4105, Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA).

The number of Ki67 staining positive cells and total epithelial cells was counted in 3~5 independent microscopic fields per mouse (n=3 mice), and the Ki67 labeling index was calculated. Submucosal invasion efficiency was assessed on the E-cadherin immunostaining sections. Masson trichrome staining was performed using Trichrome Stain (Masson) Kit (#HT15, SIGMA, St. Louis, MO). Detection of hyaluronan was performed as previously described45. Briefly, paraffin sections were incubated with Avidin/Biotin Blocking kit (#SP-2001, Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA), followed by 5μg/mL of biotinylated hyaluronan binding protein (#BC41, Hokudo CO., LTD, Sapporo, Japan) for 1 h. Staining signals were visualized using an ImmPACT DAB Peroxidase Substrate Kit (#SK-4105, Vector Laboratories) or Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated Streptavidin (#016-580-084, Jackson ImmunoResearch, West Grove, PA).

Immunocytochemistry
Cultured cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, and incubated with antibody for αSMA (#A2547, SIGMA, St. Louis, MO; 1:800), followed by Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated antibody (#A-21206, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Grand Island, NY; 1:200). DyLight 594-Phalloidin (#12877, Cell Signaling, Danvers, MA; 1:20) was used to detect F-actin.

Organoid culture
Organoids were established from mouse gastric tumors and cultured according to the previously described methods46. For each genotype, organoids were derived from both male and female mice; however, sex was not considered as a biological variable in this study because no sex-dependent differences were observed in the primary tumor phenotypes. In brief, dissected glandular stomach tissues were soaked in 5 mM EDTA at 4°C for 2 h, and the isolated glands were embedded in growth-factor-reduced (GFR) Matrigel (#356231, Corning, Corning, NY), and cultured in advanced DMEM/F-12 medium with 10 mM HEPES, 2 mM Glutamax, 1×N2, 1×B27 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA), 1 mM N-acetyl-cysteine (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), supplemented with 50 mg/ml EGF (Invitrogen), 100 ng/ml FGF10 (Peprotech, Rocky Hill, NJ), 10 nM gastrin (Sigma-Aldrich), 5 μM GSK3 inhibitor (CHIR-99021; Tocris Bioscience, Bristol, UK), 10 μM ROCK inhibitor (Y-27632; Sigma-Aldrich), and 50% of L-WRN-conditioned medium47. L-WRN cells express Wnt3a, R-spondin, and Noggin in the medium. In the absence of WRN-CM (WRN0%), 100 ng/ml Noggin (Peprotech, Cranbury, NJ) was added to the medium. Established organoid cells were treated with 1 μM of 4-hydroxy (4-OH) tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich) for 14 days to induce KTP mutations. The cell proliferation rate was examined using a CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay (#G9682; Promega, Madison, WI).

To inhibit Wnt ligand signaling, organoids were treated with 100 nM PORCN inhibitor, Wnt-C59 (C59) (S7037; Selleckchem, Houston, TX).

To label organoids, GFP cDNA was subcloned into the pPB-CAG-IP PiggyBac transposon expression vector (a gift from Dr. Hitoshi Niwa) and co-transfected with a transposase expression vector into organoid cells using Lipofectamine (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For the invasion assay, cells were seeded in Matrigel-coated Fluoroblok culture inserts with 8 μm pores (Corning). The invaded cell areas were quantified using an All-in-One microscope and BZ-II Analyzer (Keyence, Kanagawa, Japan).

Transfection and gene disruptions
To establish luciferase-expressing KTP and WKTP cells, a luciferase expression vector, pPB-CAG-Luc-IB piggyBac48, was co-transfected with a transposase expression vector (a gift from Dr. Hitoshi Niwa) using Lipofectamine LTX (#15338100, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA). The luciferase-expressing cells were selected by culture in 1 μg/mL blasticidin for 7 days.

To establish Apc-KTP cells, the pSpCas9(BB)-2A-Puro (PX459) V2.0 plasmid (#62988, Addgene) was used to package guide oligonucleotides targeting Apc. Cells were transfected with the constructed plasmid, and selected by 1 μg/mL puromycin culture for 2 days. The single-guide RNA (sgRNA) sequence is as follows: ACGGAAGTCGGGAAGGATCT.

To establish Wnt-KTP cells, mouse Wnt1 cDNA was excised from pUSEamp-Wnt1 (Upstate, Charlottesville, VA) and subcloned into pPB-CAG-IP piggyBac (a gift from Dr. Hitoshi Niwa) to construct the pPB-CAG-Wnt1-IP vector. To establish Hyal1/2-KTP cells, Hyal1 and Hyal2 cDNAs were amplified by RT-PCR. Primer sequences for RT-PCR are as follows: mHyal1-F: GCC’AAG’ACA’TGC’TTG’GGC’TTA, mHyal1-R: GTT’GGG’TGC’AGC’TAA’TCA’TCA, mHyal2-F: GAG’CTG’CTA’CCA’GGC’AGG’TA, mHyal2-R: TCC’AGG’GGG’AGA’GAT’CCC’TCA. After sequence confirmation, the Hyal1 and Hyal2 cDNA fragments were subcloned into pPB-CAG-IP piggyBac and pPB-CAG-IB piggyBac, respectively. These piggyBac vectors were co-transfected with transposase expression vector using Lipofectamine LTX (#15338100, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA), and Hyal1/Hyal2-expressing cells were selected by 1 μg/mL puromycin and 1 μg/mL blasticidin cultures for 7 days.

Organoid transplantation in mouse experiments
For orthotopic transplantation, 5×105 each of KTP or WKTP cells were transplanted into submucosa of the glandular stomach of female 6 weeks of age NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ mice (NSG mice; The Jackson Laboratory, Japan) (n=3 for each genotype), and tumor phenotypes were histologically examined at 21 days after transplantation.

For liver metastasis analysis, 5×105 each of KTP, WKTP, Apc-KTP, Wnt-KTP, or Hyal-WKTP cells were transplanted into the spleens of female 6 weeks of age NSG mice, and liver tissues were examined at 3 and 7 days (for early stage analysis), 14 days (for PORCN inhibitor treatment experiments), and 21 days after transplantation. For subcutaneous (s.c.) transplantation, 5×105 each of KTP or WKTP cells were transplanted s.c. to female 6 weeks of age Crlj:SHO-Prkdcscid Hrhr mice (SHO mice, The Jackson Laboratory, Japan), and tumor phenotypes were histologically examined at 28 days after transplantation. We used female mice for these transplantation experiments.

For inhibitor treatment experiments, WKTP cells were transplanted into the spleen, and mice were treated with PORCN inhibitors, ETC-159 (Selleckchem, Houston, TX) (30 mg/kg/day for 14 days, oral administration, p.o., n=5) or GNF-6231 (Selleckchem, Houston, TX) (3 mg/kg/day for 14 days, p.o., n=5) according to a previously described method49,50. Liver tissues were examined at 14 days after splenic transplantation with no-drug control mice (n=8).

In vivo luciferase imaging
In vivo imaging analyses were performed at 1, 2, and 3 weeks after transplantation of luciferase-expressing KTP and WKTP cells. Mice were intraperitoneally injected with 150 mg/kg D-luciferin (Fujifilm, Osaka, Japan), and liver bioluminescence was measured using IVIS Lumina LT and Living Image Software (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA).

Wnt signaling reporter assay
For measurement of Wnt signaling activity, the cells were transfected with Super 8×TOPFlash or Super 8×FOPFlash (Addgene, Cambridge, MA) using Lipofectamine LTX (Thermo Fisher). After 24 h of transfection, the luciferase activity was measured using a Dual-Luciferase Reporter assay system (Promega, Madison, WI).

Immunoblotting
Cultured cells were lysed in TNE buffer with cOmplete Mini Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (#11836170001, Roche, Basel, Switzerland), and 10 μg of the protein samples were separated using 10% SDS-polyacrylamide gel. Primary antibodies used were anti-β-catenin (#C2206, Sigma-Aldrich; 1:5000), anti-active β-catenin (#05-665, Sigma-Aldrich; 1:500), anti-TGFβ1 (#ab179695, Abcam; 1:1000), anti-Hyal1 (#25179-1-AP, Proteintech, Rosemont, IL; 1:1000), and anti-Hyal2 (#15115-1-AP, Proteintech, Rosemont, IL; 1:1000). Antibody against GAPDH (#016-25523, FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemicals, Japan; 1:2000) was used for internal control. The ECL detection system (#RPN2235, GE Healthcare, Buckinghamshire, UK) was used to detect immunoblotting signals. Band intensities of active β-catenin were measured using ImageJ software (v1.52, NIH, Bethesda, MD) and normalized with those of GAPDH. Uncropped and unprocessed scans of blots are provided as a Source Data file.

HSC and CAF culture experiments
Hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) were isolated from C57BL/6 or Trp53 LSL-R270H mouse livers according to the protocol51. Trp53 LSL-R270H-derived HSCs were established as immortalized HSCs (imHSCs). Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were isolated from liver metastasized tumors in Trp53 LSL-R270H mice transplanted with intestinal tumor-derived AKTP cells19. The primary HSCs, imHSCs, and CAFs were stimulated with 10% Afamin-Wnt3a (#J2-001, MBL, Tokyo, Japan) and/or 20 ng/mL recombinant mouse TGFβ1 (#7666-MB, R&D, Minneapolis, MN) for 48 h.

For PCR Array analysis, the cDNA was synthesized using RT2 First Strand Kit (#330401, Qiagen GmbH, Hilden, Germany), and expression of Wnt-target genes was examined using the RT2 Profiler PCR Array Mouse WNT Signaling Targets (#PAMM-243ZD, Qiagen GmbH, Hilden, Germany). The statistical significance of the expression data was analyzed using the GeneGlobe Data Analysis Center (https://geneglobe.qiagen.com/us/analyze/).

For contraction assay, 1×106 HSCs were suspended in 1 mL ECM gel [Cell matrix Type I-A (Nitta gelatin, Japan): Matrigel (Corning) = 3:1], transferred to a 24-well plate, and allowed to solidify at 37°C for 30 min. Then, 10% Afamin-Wnt3a and/or TGFβ1 were added to the culture medium, and the size of the ECM disks was measured at 48 h.

RT-PCR analysis
Total RNA was extracted from the primary HSCs, imHSCs, and CAFs using Isogen (Nippon Gene, Toyama, Japan), reverse-transcribed using a PrimeScript RT reagent Kit (＃RR081, Takara Bio, Otsu, Japan), and amplified using TB Green Premix Ex Taq II (＃RR820, Takara Bio, Otsu, Japan) in an AriaMx real-time thermocycler (Agilent Technologies). Relative mRNA levels of Has2 and Acta2 to those of Gapdh were calculated. The primer sequences are indicated as follows: Alb-F: TTGCAAGGCTGCTGACAAGG, Alb-R: TTTAGGCTAAGGCGTCTTTGCATC, Prom1-F: TGTTAATGGCATTCTGTGTGGCTA, Prom1-R: CCTCTGAATCCATCCTGCGATA, Muc1-F: AAGAGCTATGGGCAGCTGGAC, Muc1-R: TCACCACAGCTGGGTTGGTATAA, Acta2-F: GACAATGGCTCTGGGCTCTGTA, Acta2-R: TTTGGCCCATTCCAACCATTA, Has2-F: TGTGAGAGGTTTCTATGTGTCCT, Has2-R: ACCGTACAGTCCAAATGAGAAGT, Gapdh-F: GGCACAGTCAAGGCTGAGAATG, Gapdh-R: ATGGTGGTGAAGACGCCAGTA

Spatial transcriptomic analysis
Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples passing the RNA quality control (DV200>50%) were used for spatial transcriptomic construction and sequencing. The tissue was prepared according to the Visium CytAssist Special Gene Expression for FFPE-Tissue Preparation Guide (10X Genomics, Pleasanton, CA). The sequencing was performed by the Research Institute for Microbial Diseases at Osaka University. Libraries were sequenced on an MGI DNBSEQ-G400RS (MGI Tech Co, Shenzhen, China). Raw spatial transcriptomics data were processed using the Space Ranger pipeline (v2.0.1, 10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA), aligned to the mm10-2020-A mouse reference genome, and analyzed from the resulting FASTQ files. For downstream analysis, including UMAP visualization, violin plots, and gene expression analysis, we used Loupe Browser v6.0 (10x Genomics). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using 100 dimensions.

The cell-type-specific marker genes were extracted using the PanglaoDB database (https://panglaodb.se/)52. Upstream regulators were examined using the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) (Ingenuity Systems, QIAGEN Digital Insights). A Z-score of ≥2 and a p-value of <0.05 were considered to indicate activation with statistical significance.

Database analysis
The genetic alterations, including mutations, structural variants, copy number variations, and mRNA overexpression in WNTs and HAS2, were analyzed in 440 stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) samples from the TCGA PanCancer Atlas using the cBioPortal database (https://www.cbioportal.org/). Samples with an mRNA expression Z-score of 1 or higher across all STAD samples in the genomic profile were considered to exhibit overexpression. Expression levels in these samples were confirmed to be more than twice as high as those in the other samples. The distribution of genetic alterations in WNTs and HAS2 was analyzed using OncoPrint in cBioPortal. Additionally, co-expression analysis between HAS2 and ECM components, as well as between HAS2 and WNTs, was performed using cBioPortal, with Spearman’s correlation applied. Genes related to extracellular matrix (ECM) components and the collagen family were extracted using QuickGO (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/QuickGO/).

Statistical analyses
The data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (s.d.). The statistical analysis was performed using two-sided unpaired t-tests or a one-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test. Excel (version 16.94, Microsoft) and GraphPad Prism 9 were used for these analyses. A one-sided Fisher’s exact test was used to calculate P-values of overlap in Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. P-values of <0.05 were considered statistically significant.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors identified a new role for WNT ligands in promoting liver metastasis of gastric cancer, utilizing genetically engineered organoids, transplantation models, and spatial transcriptomics (Visium). It was proposed that canonical Wnt ligands (specifically Wnt1) secreted by tumor cells upregulate hyaluronan synthase, Has2, in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) derived from hepatic stellate cells, thereby promoting liver metastasis. This is an interesting study that unveils an unexpected role of canonical WNT ligands in establishing a tumor-favoring metastatic niche. However, several points warrant further attention through new experimental results, discussion, and tone adjustments.

Major comments
1. Orthotopic vs. intrasplenic transplantation. With the exception of gastric tumor analysis (Figure 2), the authors performed intrasplenic injection of organoids instead of orthotopic transplantation. Consequently, this study does not provide direct evidence on whether orthotopic injection of KTP or WKTP organoids into the stomach would result in metastasis to other organs. It is necessary to assess whether orthotopically injected organoids/cells give rise to distant metastases, particularly to the liver, followed by repeating key experiments shown in Figures 3-7 using orthotopic models.
2. Immunocompetent vs. immunocompromised mice: The authors utilized NSG and SHO mice for transplantations. Given that KTP and WKTP organoids were derived from C57BL/6 mice, syngeneic transplantation in C57BL/6 mice could offer a more pathophysiologically relevant immune environment. Could the authors clarify their rationale for choosing an immunodeficient background instead? Considering the aforementioned point (#1), performing orthotopic transplantation of organoids (or organoid-derived cells) in C57BL/6 mice is necessary. Alternatively, investigating liver metastasis in the genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs) (Figure 1) could also be considered, as the authors described in the Introduction (lines 92-96; notably, this GEMM was not used to study metastasis in this manuscript).
3. Mechanisms: How does WNT/β-catenin signaling convert HSCs into CAFs and upregulate Has1/2? More discussion is needed.
4. HAS2 blockade in tumor cells (performed in this manuscript) vs. CAFs (not presented): Instead of Hyal expression in WKTP, HAS2 blockade in CAFs would be ideal. Thus, tone adjustment or further discussion is recommended.
5. Pathological relevance: The study focuses on liver metastasis, but GC is known to metastasize to various organs, including the peritoneum, lymph nodes, and lungs. The authors must clarify whether liver metastasis is the most clinically relevant metastatic site for GCs expressing canonical Wnt ligands.

Minor comments
1. The Rationale for selecting Wnt1 (over other ligands, including Wnt3a and Wnt5a). This study mentioned the role of ligand-dependent Wnt signaling in GC, and Wnt1 was specifically chosen for transgenic expression in the mouse model. However, it remains unclear why Wnt1 was selected over Wnt3a or Wnt5a. The authors need to provide literature, dataset, or experimental results-based justification for prioritizing Wnt1. Additionally, is there any transcriptomic or patient-derived data supporting WNT1 as the dominant Wnt ligand in liver-metastatic gastric cancer or a CIN-subtype? It should be noted that Wnt5a is a non-canonical WNT ligand. Similarly, in line 278, it is necessary to separate canonical vs. non-canonical WNT ligands since this study suggests the crucial role of canonical WNT ligands in liver metastasis.
2. Figures 6 and 7: What is the primary source of TGF-beta to activate CAFs and upregulate HAS in conjunction with canonical WNT ligands?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript demonstrates that Wnt ligand-dependent signaling promotes metastasis of chromosomal instability (CIN) subtype gastric cancer to liver through increasing hyaluronan expression in the metastatic tumor microenvironment. This study used multiple mouse models with mutations driven by Claudin18-IRES-CreERT2, inducing Tgfbr2flox/flox, Trp53LSL·R270H, KrasLSL·G12D, and K19-Wnt1. The organoids derived from these mouse models highlighted that Wnt1 signaling activation is required for efficient liver metastasis in stromal cells.

The current manuscript could be the first study detailing the potential mechanism of how stromal Wnt1 promotes CIN gastric cancer metastasis via Has2. The experiments are very nicely illustrated, and the data are almost all of high quality. The paper is also clearly written. However, there are several concerns that should be addressed:
1. The study used a tamoxifen (Tam) concentration of 4mg/mouse to induce CreERT2 at 6 weeks of age. Tam at this concentration can cause parietal cell loss and induce chief cells to go through spasmolytic polypeptide-expressing metaplasia (SPEM). Authors should discuss the possible stomach epithelial injury resulting from use of Tam at this concentration and its potential impacts on their gastric cancer genetic engineered mouse model and cite the relevant papers: PMID: 22001866, 27246044, 31233898. It is possible the metaplasia caused by Tam helps give a headstart to the lesions/tumors.
2. How did the authors activate CreERT2 in vitro? Tamoxifen is usually not miscible in tissue culture media, so most people use 4-hydroxy tamoxifen instead of tamoxifen.
3. In Figure 1A, authors should clarify the time needed for Tam to induce KTP mutations in organoids. Also, “KP” is an error, as it is the same as “KT”.
4. For the invasive lesions in Fig. 1, how confident are the authors that the glandular forms found, especially solitary ones are actually invasive? Because when there is marked hyperplasia of mouse stomach, the tissue can be distorted such that glands can twist around and be cut in cross-section, appearing pseudo-invasive. Although the image is small, it does look as though the single gland invasion in 1G is invasive, because there is distortion of surrounding stromal cells, and there seems to be an actual tumor (mass) formed, but this call can be tricky in many cases.
5. There seems to be a loss of Muc5AC-positivity in the pit zone of Wnt-expressing tumor mice. What makes up the pit in these mice? Is there a reason why overexpression of Wnt would block foveolar cell differentiation?
6. The mouse genetics are a bit unclear. Is the Trp53R270H allele kept as a heterozygote with the other, endogenous Trp53 allele wild-type? Presumably, the Kras gain of function is an LSL?
7. Figure 2C is missing the statistical analysis.
8. Figure 3 and Figure 4: for the KTP/WKTP/Apc-KTP/Wnt-KTP spleen injection experiment, besides in the liver, is there any other organ metastasis? Especially in the WKTP group, the liver metastasis phenotype is very strong as shown in Figure 4F.
Figure 3A: typo, “speen” should be “spleen”.
9. Figure 3F: needs to show the representative H&E images of tumor area/field. Moreover, how are we to interpret reproducibility/statistics here? One control mouse is lower than all 3 in GNF. Are the datapoints means from many tumor areas/fields in a single mouse? There is no stat analysis here either.
10. Figure 3H: authors used GFP to trace tumor cells. But where is the GFP coming from? Authors did not mention the use of GFP in the mouse strains. Authors should clarify all the detailed genotypes of the mouse strains used in current manuscript (W, K, KT, KP, KTGP, WKT, WKP, WKTP).
11. Figure 4C needs to label the protein size (kDa). Why not western blot for APC and Wnt1?
12. Figure 4F/Supplementary Figure 5B experiment need the β-catenin IHC staining results. Are there more nuclear β-catenin in stromal cells in the Wnt-KTP group compared to KTP or Apc-KTP groups?
13. The labels among the groups in Figure 4F and Figure 4G are confusing. There is one group of KTP mice in Figure 4F, but with two columns for KTP mice (#1,2) shown in Figure 4G; and one group of WKTP mice in Figure 4F but with three columns shown in Figure 4G (#1,2,3). In Figure 4F, the KTP and WKTP image section is missing a scale bar.
14. The authors should perform a transwell assay to test the cell invasion ability among KTP, WKTP, Apc-KTP, and Wnt-KTP groups.
15. Supplementary Figure 5A is missing Wnt-KTP cell data. How did authors reach the conclusion that “the proliferation rates of Apc-KTP and Wnt-KTP cells were unchanged compared to parental KTP cells”?
16. Figure 5B, 5D and Supplementary Figure 6 are missing a scale bar.
17. “Hepatocyte marker Alb was significantly increased in cluster 3 and 6, while epithelial markers, Ceacam1 and Muc1, were increased…” Technically, liver is epithelium also, so this should be clarified, because it is not clear which epithelial markers were used or why the ones shown are the representative epithelial cell markers.
18. The authors should show representative IHC image results (translational level) to validate the spatial transcriptomic data (transcriptional level), for CTNNB1, WNT3A, TGFB1, SAMD3, and SMAD4.
19. In Figure 7A, Has2 is not limited to cluster 5, which raises the question of whether the authors have performed the filtering before analyzing the spatial transcriptomic data by using Loupe Browser? The authors did not mention how they processed the spatial transcriptomic data. This should be detailed.
20. The authors mention HA interacting with CD44 on stem cells and hypothesize the same sort of interaction in gastric cancer, but there is a paper that does show that metaplasia in stomach expands CD44+ progenitor cells that as HA expands, so this paper should be cited and potentially discussed: PMID:23589310. There are other papers detailing CD44 role in metaplasia and stemness in stomach (eg, PMID: 31071489), so the CD44/xCT/HA pathway may be important in both metaplasia and metastasis.
21. A visualization of cell-cell communication, using differentially expressed genes (DEGs), would greatly improve analysis, as one would expect important cell-cell communication between cluster 5 and the rest of the clusters. For example, as the authors state, CD44 in tumor cells could be communicating with HA in stroma.
